title: SecTor 2025 | Chasing Shadows: Chronicles of Counter-Intelligence from the Citizen Lab

segments.text: So yeah, I'm a professor of political
science, not computer science, but I am
the founder and director of the Citizen
Lab at the University of Toronto. And if
you know nothing else about the Citizen
Lab, you probably heard about our
research into NSO group and its Pegasus
spyware. Over the last several decades,
we've uh published reports,
investigations into the abuse of
mercenary spyware and have found in just
about every region of the world
governments abusing this type of
technology to go after political
opposition, dissident, activists and
others. And this has generated a lot of
publicity and media worldwide. Uh
probably the biggest case for us in
terms of exposure started with this
fellow uh Omar Abdul Aziz. Uh he's a
Canadian permanent resident, a Saudi who
came to Canada to study in the early
2010s. And um he became an activist
around the time of the Arab Spring,
started a big YouTube channel where he's
criticizing the Saudi human rights
record and Muhammad bin Salman directly.
uh he was a close confidant and and
friend of uh Washington Post journalist
Jamal Hashoi and uh they had been
communicating uh over WhatsApp what they
uh quite rightly assumed would be secure
endto-end encrypted messaging app and
they were basically organizing kind of
social media enabled activism
and uh although they were a little
paranoid as you can see from a brief
snippet of this conversation they didn't
realize
until we discovered uh that Omar
Abdulaziz's phone was hacked with NSO
group's Pegasus spyware that the whole
time that they were communicating uh
Saudi intelligence agents were
essentially eavesdropping over many many
months on that conversation. Uh we
published our report on the hacking of
Omar's phone October 1st, 2018. October
2nd, Jamal went into the Saudi consulate
in Istanbul, uh, Turkey, and of course
was, uh, met with a kill squad from
Saudi Arabia that murdered him and
executed him. Um, that was a very
important case for us. And, uh, if you u
speak to the industry or you read about
reports like this, this is a familiar
refrain you get from them. This is a
quote from the former CEO of NSO Group,
Shallov Julio. If you're not a criminal,
don't be afraid. Our technology is very
strictly controlled to help governments
investigate serious matters of crime,
terrorism, national security. Well, the
big takeaway of the Citizen Lab's
research over the last uh one and a half
decades is actually you should be uh
very afraid. So, a bit more about the
Citizen Lab for those of you who don't
know. As I said, we're founded in 2001.
We do research on digital security
issues that arise out of human rights
concerns. So um we do work that's
probably very similar to a lot of you
who are in the threat intelligence space
in this room methodologically in terms
of the tools we use, the approaches we
take. The big difference is of course
we're not trying to sell you anything.
We're an academic research group. We see
what we're doing as being in the public
interest. So we do these evidence-based
research reports to try to raise
awareness and we're also uh filling a
gap. So uh there is uh a market failure
if you will when it comes to cyber
security for what I would call civil
society. So you have the private sector,
you have governments and then you have
basically everybody else. And it's that
everybody else where there's a major gap
because most NOS's, most human rights
organizations, even small independent
media organizations, they simply can't
afford to hire some of the very, you
know, impressive companies down in that
showroom because they don't have the
budget. And so they're left exposed. And
yet it's those organizations that face
the very same advanced p persistent
threats that a lot of the threat
intelligence companies focus on and
protect the private sector and
governments from. So we see ourselves
doing a kind of digital accountability
role. Um when I founded the lab I
described what we're doing as counter
intelligence for civil society. And at
that time in 2001 frankly that was a
little aspirational shall we say. And if
you fast forward to today, uh I think
that's exactly what we do. And the old
adage comes to mind, uh careful what you
wish for, as I'll explain in a few
minutes. Um now, you may not realize,

Ghostnet report which exposed a major
China based espionage operation

And so we, you know, kind of bandied
around. We said ghostnet. So for those

all these threat actor names, I guess
you can blame us to some extent because
that was really the first of them. Um,
in terms of first as well, we at the
citizen lab have produced the first
evidence-based reports on some of the uh
major spyware vendors out there on in

Uh in terms of important cases for us
